newsitem.title: CANADA: British Columbia calls for salmon counterattack.
newsitem.headline: British Columbia calls for salmon counterattack.

text.p: British Columbia on Wednesday urged Ottawa to let Canadian fishermen intercept Pacific salmon headed toward U.S. waters, as a way of intensifying pressure on the United States to settle a fishing dispute.

British Columbia Premier Glen Clark called on Canada's federal Fisheries Minister David Anderson to implement a "Canada First" fishing plan that was developed by a joint federal-provincial technical working group.

"It is absolutely essential that we structure our fishing plans this season to defend British Columbia stocks and ensure Americans do not benefit from their refusal to negotiate a renewed Pacific salmon treaty," Clark said.

Canada and the United States have been squabbling for four years over how to divide Pacific salmon catches. Tensions reached the boiling point recently and angry Canadian fishermen last week blockaded an Alaska ferry to highlight their claims that Alaskans were overfishing.

Clark said the "Canada First" plan proposes various options to maximize conservation of Canadian salmon "while ensuring Canadians harvest any available surplus that could otherwise be taken by American fishing fleets."

Under one leading scenario, Canadian fishing boats could congregate in southern British Columbia near the boundary between Canadian and U.S. waters and catch salmon that might otherwise head into the nets of U.S. fishermen.
British Columbia officials said this would be similar to the approach used by Alaskan fishermen in the north which resulted in catches of sockeye salmon several times higher than normal.
The salmon fishing season has already begun in Alaska and northern British Columbia and is due to start in earnest in southern British Columbia and Washington over the next weeks.

Ottawa has expressed interest in expanding fishing in southern British Columbia this year because of the salmon dispute with the United States, but it was not clear when a decision on the plan would be announced. Federal officials were not immediately available for comment.

After meetings in Washington on Tuesday, Anderson was due to meet the governors of Alaska and Washington later on Wednesday in Seattle. Clark said he expected the fishing proposals to have "a big impact on negotiations" with the United States.

Other options proposed by the working group included filing lawsuits against the United States and charging a transit fee to U.S. boats using the popular Inside Passage waterway between Vancouver Island and the mainland.
